title: Follow 100 people, or two clues?
hook: Clues are right 2 times in 3. 100 people chose blue. How much do they know?

knows: two-said-blue: after a lead of 2, people ignore their own clue
doesNotKnow: that a cascade of 100 followers carries only the first two clues, so two public clues can overturn it

misconception: A choice followed by 100 people is backed by 100 people's evidence.
objective: The learner can explain that the 98 followers in a cascade add no evidence, so the 100 blue choices hold only 2 clues, and two published red clues plus their own red clue make red the better choice (blue falls to 33%).

claims.text: In a cascade, from person 3 on a lead of 2 outweighs any single clue, so people after the first two follow regardless of their own clue and their choices reveal nothing: the 98 followers chose blue because of the first two choices, not their own clues.
claims.source: Easley and Kleinberg (2010) ch. 16 (information cascades; sections unconfirmed); S. Bikhchandani, D. Hirshleifer and I. Welch (1992), 'A Theory of Fads, Fashion, Custom, and Cultural Change as Informational Cascades', J. Political Economy 100(5). Attribution: fact-checker confirms (flag carried from the brief). Stage stub: 'Person 3 on: a lead of 2 wins'. | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Verified by derivation, not by the sources: E&K ch. 16 and BHW 1992 were NOT opened (every scholarly host was unreachable through the proxy). With q = 2/3 and prior 1/2, person 3 holds 2 inferred blue clues. Own red gives P(blue) = 2/3 > 1/2, and own blue gives 8/9, so person 3 picks blue either way and the choice carries no clue. By induction every later person faces the same 2-clue lead (own node, persons 3-100, no break). The stage line 'Person 3 on: a lead of 2 wins' and reveal para 1 match.

claims.text: With clues right 2 times in 3 and even odds to start, 2 blue clues and 3 red clues give the blue urn a 33% chance, so red is the better choice.
claims.source: Bayes with likelihood ratio 2 per clue: P(blue) = 1 / (1 + 2^(red − blue)) = 1 / (1 + 2) = 1/3. pBlue in Demo.tsx, builder re-run in node 2026-10-14; matches the brief's node check (0.333). | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Demo pBlue(b, r) = 1 / (1 + 2^(r - b)) equals the exact Bayes posterior for q = 2/3 and prior 1/2 (own node: both give 0.3333 for 2 blue and 3 red). The readout shows 33% and 'Best: red', and the reveal says 'blue falls to 33%, and red is the better choice'. Advisory: the prior of 1/2 ('even odds') is never stated to the learner; only the hook gives the 2-in-3 accuracy.

claims.text: Without the published clues, the same person with a red clue in the cascade still rates blue at 67%.
claims.source: 2 blue clues vs 1 red: 1 / (1 + 2^(1 − 2)) = 2/3. pBlue(2, 1) in Demo.tsx, builder re-run 2026-10-14; matches the brief (inCascadeOwnRed 0.667). | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. pBlue(2, 1) = 2/3, shown as 67%: the readout after counting and before publishing. The log 'Before publishing: 67% blue' and reveal 'With your red clue alone, blue stayed at 67%' match. Exact Bayes gives 0.6667.

claims.text: The 100 blue choices held only 2 clues; a herd built on two clues can be overturned by two more.
claims.source: Follows from c1–c3: only persons 1–2 chose on their own clue, so the crowd's evidence is 2 blue clues; adding 2 red clues (plus the learner's own red) moves blue from 67% to 33%. | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Follows from c1-c3: persons 1-2 are the only ones who chose on their own clues, so the 100 choices hold 2 clues. The reveal puts 'overturned by two more' right after 'Two published red clues plus yours make 3 red to 2 blue', and with the learner's own red clue it flips to 33%. Note: without the learner's red clue, two red against two blue is 50%, a tie, not a reversal. The sentence holds only in its reveal context (see the new c6).

The lesson's model (brief two-public-clues-break-the-herd, company/domains/briefs/probability.statistics.md, Course: NCM: clues right 2/3 of the time, prior 1/2), carried over from two-said-blue. | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. The hook (meta.json, learner-facing) reads 'Clues are right 2 times in 3.', and pBlue uses likelihood ratio 2 = (2/3)/(1/3). It is a stated model convention.

claims.text: The packed room rests on two opinions, so two independent new ones count as much as the whole crowd, and one more would tip it.
claims.source: UNRECORDED CLAIM found by fact-checker (pass 23, 2026-10-14); the sentence is the builder's, recorded here word for word (meta.json recall.why, second sentence). | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): DISPUTED. Recall card 'why' (meta.json recall.why), learner-visible after the lesson. In the lesson's own model (equally reliable clues, prior 1/2), two new clues against the two the crowd holds give 1 / (1 + 2^0) = 50%: they cancel it, they do not outweigh it. The recall scenario has no own clue to tip it, unlike the reveal. 'Can' would need critics more reliable than diners, which the card does not say. Fix (builder): 'two independent new ones can cancel it out, and one more would tip it', or 'two independent new ones count as much as the whole crowd'. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v2, wave E r6 revision by demo-builder): reworded per pass 23: two equally reliable new clues cancel the crowd's two (50%), they do not outweigh it; a third tips it. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. Lesson model P(blue) = 1 / (1 + 2^(red - blue)): crowd's 2 vs 2 new = 50% (count as much), 2 vs 3 = 33% (tips it). Pass 23 dispute resolved by the rewording. Assumes the new clues are as reliable as the diners' (the lesson's equal-reliability model).

recall.question: A restaurant is packed because the first two diners picked it and everyone after them followed the crowd. Two food critics then independently pan it. How much should the crowd outweigh the critics?
options: A lot: hundreds of diners chose it
Not much: the crowd carries only the first two diners' information
Not at all: crowds are always wrong
recall.why: Followers in a cascade copy the people ahead of them, so their choices add no new information. The packed room rests on two opinions, so two independent new ones count as much as the whole crowd, and one more would tip it.
